name: North and South Kinsman

legs.route: Lonesome Lake Trail, Fishin' Jimmy Trail, then the Kinsman Ridge Trail
Kinsman Ridge Trail
legs.connect: Follow the wooded ridge trail onward to the second summit, which carries the cairn.

how: Both summits sit on one ridge trail, so they are done together from the campground in the notch. The approach passes a lake and a hut, then the middle trail climbs in many short ups and downs before the ridge. North comes first on the way out, and the same trail returns over it. Winter parties need microspikes or snowshoes depending on depth, and one steep icy stretch lies on the middle trail.
descent: Retrace over North Kinsman, then down the middle trail and the lake trail to the lot. The out-and-back is the common plan.
logistics: Park at the campground lot in the notch. Water is available at the hut near the lake in season. Expect about 10 miles round trip.
notes: Second source is a winter report that does not state order or mileage. Gain not stated by either page.

name: Mount Osceola and East Osceola

legs.route: Mount Osceola Trail
Short ridge trail from Osceola, past the Chimney
legs.connect: Drop into the col by the trail, taking either the bypass or the steep rock step known as the Chimney, then climb to the wooded second summit.

how: Osceola is climbed first on a rocky trail with almost no views. From its top the trail dips to a col and then climbs to East Osceola, which is forested; the leg takes about 45 minutes each way. A near-vertical step called the Chimney sits on this connector. Some parties bypass it going down and take it going back up, since the climb is easier than the descent.
descent: Come back over the same ground to Osceola, then down the Mount Osceola Trail. The long stony descent is hard on knees, so poles help.
logistics: Start from the Mount Osceola trailhead. Reports list roughly 8 miles round trip and about 3,000 feet of gain for the pair.
notes: Distance and gain from the first page only (8.4 mi, 3,000 ft); the second left them blank.

name: North and South Hancock loop

legs.route: Hancock Notch Trail, Cedar Brook Trail, then the Hancock Loop Trail
Hancock Loop Trail along the ridge
legs.connect: Walk the short ridge between the two, crossing muddy patches (a bypass path exists) and gaining a few hundred feet.

how: A flat approach on the notch trail leads to a side trail and then a loop whose two arms climb to the two summits. Either direction is done: the right-hand arm is a direct climb to South, the left arm drops to cross a drainage before climbing North. The ridge between them is gentle with soft footing and deep mud in spots. Both summits are wooded with short side paths to viewpoints.
descent: Return from the second summit down the loop trail to the split, then out the side trail and notch trail to the road. Only the loop part avoids retracing.
logistics: Trailhead is on the pass road east of the town of Lincoln. The approach crosses a brook about five times, which can be hard at high water. Roughly 9 miles round trip.
notes: Direction differs: one report went South then North, the other two did North then South. Leg order shown is the clockwise one; reversible. Gain not stated by any page.

name: Tripyramids (North, Middle, South) loop

legs.route: North Slide, from Livermore Road via the Mount Tripyramid Trail
Mount Tripyramid Trail along the ridge
legs.connect: Follow the ridge trail south, about a mile, mostly in trees with one viewpoint near the middle summit.

legs.route: Mount Tripyramid Trail
legs.connect: Continue a short distance, under half a mile, to the last summit.

how: The classic loop climbs the North Slide, a steep open scramble of ledge and loose rock, then follows the ridge over all three summits and drops the South Slide. Going up the north side and down the south is preferred because the south slide is eroded gravel better descended than climbed. The north slide should not be tried when wet, and rockfall onto people below is a risk.
descent: Descend the South Slide, steep and loose, then rejoin the valley trail and walk the long, flat woods road back to the lot. This makes a loop rather than a repeat of the ascent.
logistics: Parking is at the road lot, with a day fee. The woods road is about 3.6 miles each way. Total about 11 miles and 3,000 feet of gain.
notes: Both pages agree on about 11 miles and 3,000 ft. A longer alternative onto the ridge for those avoiding the slide appeared only in search results; not included.

name: Wildcat Ridge (Wildcat A to D)

legs.route: Wildcat Ridge Trail, with a bushwhack to the true high point
Wildcat Ridge Trail
legs.connect: Walk the ridge over the small rounded intermediate summits (B and C), about two miles.

how: The two 4,000-foot summits are the ends of one ridge trail, with two lower bumps between them. From the road side the climb is steep with boulders and some rock steps for the first miles, then reaches the top of the ski area where a lift ends. The ridge itself is mostly gentle but rough underfoot. The two middle bumps are crossed without marked summits.
descent: Either retrace the ridge to the road, or drop from A steeply to the notch and walk out on the brook trail, or set a car shuttle at the far end. Winter parties usually take D first, then A.
logistics: Two lots are used: the falls lot across the highway, or the ski area lodge when a car is spotted. Allow about six hours for the ridge; the notch hut offers water.
notes: Reports run both directions (A first from the notch side, D first from the highway side); order shown is the highway-side start. A 287 ft gain figure in one page is inconsistent so omitted; loop with car spot about 9.7 miles, out and back about 8.4.

name: Carter-Moriah Traverse (with the Wildcats)
region: Carter Range, Wildcat Ridge, Pinkham Notch

legs.route: Wildcat Ridge Trail from the highway lot (optional: the traverse can start at the notch)
Wildcat Ridge Trail
legs.connect: Cross the ridge over the bumps in between, then continue.

legs.route: Carter-Moriah Trail from Carter Notch
legs.connect: Drop steeply to the notch hut, then climb about a mile on rough trail to a wooded summit.

legs.route: Carter-Moriah Trail (optional spur; a bypass skips it)
legs.connect: Follow the ridge to the bald summit with the best views, then descend steeply.

legs.route: Carter-Moriah Trail
legs.connect: Follow easy grades along the wooded crest past an alpine meadow.

legs.route: Carter-Moriah Trail
legs.connect: Descend a steep boulder and wet slab section to the col with the shelter, then climb to a ledgy summit.

how: A south-to-north ridge crossing of some 19 miles that strings the two Wildcat 4000-footers, a notch, and the Carter chain into one line. The Wildcat Ridge is the roughest, with boulders and steep rock steps; the Carters are easy by comparison; the drops off Hight and North Carter are steep. Some do only the Carter part from the notch trail. Many plans stop at the notch hut or camp at the shelter.
descent: Finish by a long trail off Moriah to the town side. Alternatives are bail-outs down the Imp trail or the Stony Brook trail.
logistics: A shuttle or bike is needed between the highway lot and the far trailhead. Water at the notch hut and a spring near Carter Dome. Times vary widely: runners about five hours, hikers 11 or more.
notes: Distance 17.9 to 19.2 miles, gain 5,700 to 7,400 ft; omitted from prose. The 2008 report started at the notch trail, skipping the Wildcats. The FKT page standard direction is north to south.

name: Seward Range (Seward, Donaldson, Emmons)

legs.route: Herd path from the Blueberry side
Herd path along the ridge
legs.connect: Drop to the col and climb the next summit on the same path.

legs.route: Herd path
legs.connect: Continue along the ridge to the third summit, then return to Donaldson.

how: Three High Peaks on one ridge, reached by unmarked herd paths. Climbers either camp at a lean-to near the trailhead and do all three on one long day, or carry overnight gear over Seward and Donaldson, drop it, take Emmons and return. The brook herd path is considered the best route on and off the ridge, but it means doubling back over Donaldson. Mud and blowdown are the main troubles.
descent: Many come down the way they went, over Seward and out to the truck trail. Others use the brook herd path from the Donaldson area, which is easier but ends away from the Blueberry trail.
logistics: Trail access is by a long truck road; lean-tos and tent sites near the trailhead make a base. Seymour Mountain is often a separate second-day trip.
notes: Both pages are informal: a 2005 planning thread and a one-person report that also did Seymour the next day. Mileage not stated anywhere; omitted.

name: Giant and Rocky Peak Ridge traverse
region: Adirondack High Peaks, Giant Mountain Wilderness

legs.route: Trail from the Chapel Pond side (past the Washbowl) or from the falls
Ridge trail from Giant
legs.connect: Drop to the col, then climb gradually along the ridge over rocky and open terrain.

how: The two peaks form a ridge, so they are done as a one-way traverse. West to east is the usual line: climb Giant first, then cross to Rocky Peak Ridge, then descend a long trail through open land to the far road. Slab scrambling near Giant's top, a steep muddy drop into the col, and a long dry day with scarce water are the main issues.
descent: From Rocky Peak Ridge descend an east-side trail past a pond to a notch, then, in the longer version, climb a third bump before dropping to the trailhead. This ends at a different road than the start.
logistics: Needs two cars or a swap with another party. Little reliable water, so carry plenty; the pond water is brown.
notes: Start trailhead differs (falls vs Chapel Pond trail); one page adds Bald Peak and Blueberry Cobbles, the other only Bald Peak. Distances and gain not stated; omitted.

name: Hamlin Peak and Baxter Peak (Katahdin) loop

legs.route: Chimney Pond Trail, Cathedral Trail, then the Saddle Trail
Saddle Trail, Northwest Basin Trail, then the Hamlin Ridge Trail
legs.connect: Cross the flat tableland north from the high point to the second summit.

how: The two Katahdin summits are joined by an easy walk across the tableland, so the pair is a loop from the roadhead. One plan climbs the rocky Hamlin Ridge first and comes down by the saddle; another goes up to Baxter and comes down Hamlin Ridge. The ridge trail is steep with big boulders and hand-over-foot sections, and junctions are many, so a map is needed.
descent: Descend the Hamlin Ridge or the saddle trail to the pond, then walk the pond trail back to the campground. The descent route differs from the climb.
logistics: Day-use parking is limited and reserved ahead; camping needs a booking and dogs are not allowed. The lower saddle trail may be closed in early season by snow.
notes: The forum report did Baxter then Hamlin; the newspaper page describes the Hamlin-only loop and mentions Baxter only in passing, so the pairing on one page is the forum report plus search listings of other reports. Mileage 10.1 only from the second; omitted. DROPPED by reviewer: only one page covers the pair.

name: Bigelow Range traverse

legs.route: Long-distance trail from the east road (some skip it)
Long-distance trail
legs.connect: Climb past a boulder field and cliffs on the main trail.

legs.route: Long-distance trail
legs.connect: Descend through the col, then climb the highest of the range.

legs.route: Long-distance trail along the ridge
legs.connect: Walk the exposed ridge about two miles, then a steep final climb.

legs.route: Blue-blaze side trail (end of the full range)
legs.connect: On a full crossing, continue over a side trail to the last peak.

how: A crossing of the whole massif that is both a one-day endurance outing and a backpacking trip. Two peaks pass 4,000 feet and the rest are lesser summits. The full line follows one main trail with side trails to the camps. Terrain is steep and rocky with long wooded ridges, waterless stretches and open, windy tops.
descent: Descend a gentle woods trail from the horn area to the road below, or finish over Cranberry to the road on the town side. Winter access may require skiing part of the road.
logistics: Two cars are needed for a one-way crossing. Camps include a notch tentsite and a pond site with lean-tos; a bear warning applied to the notch site. Count on about 16 to 17 miles for the whole line.
notes: The forum trip went east to west and ended at South Horn; the FKT page runs it the other way and adds Cranberry via a blue-blaze trail. Route names are generic because pages only say main trail. Gain 6,850 to roughly 10,000 ft; omitted.
